note: Pre-generated demo hints for the public GitHub Pages demo. Written by an AI coding agent (Devin) from the problem statements; no live LLM call and no API key in the browser.

atcoder:abc172_c.title: ABC172 C. Tsundoku
levels: You always read a prefix of desk A and a prefix of desk B. Once you fix how many books you take from A, what is the best you can do on B?

Prefix sums + two pointers (or binary search). As the number of books taken from A grows, the longest affordable prefix of B can only shrink, so a single pointer moving backwards is enough. Classic WA: forgetting the case of taking 0 books from A.

1. Build prefix sums SA[0..N] and SB[0..M] in 64-bit.
2. j = M. For i = 0..N: if SA[i] > K stop; while SB[j] > K − SA[i], decrement j; ans = max(ans, i + j).
3. Print ans. O(N + M).

atcoder:abc175_c.title: ABC175 C. Walking Takahashi
levels: Values go up to 10^15, so simulating every move is impossible. Walking toward 0 is clearly right until you would overshoot — what do the remaining moves do after that?
Work with |X|. Take q = min(K, |X| / D) steps toward zero. If moves remain, you can only bounce between r = |X| − qD and r − D, so only the parity of the remaining moves matters.

1. X = |X|.
2. q = min(K, X / D); X −= q·D; K −= q.
3. If K is even print X, else print D − X.
Never compute K·D directly — it overflows 64-bit. O(1).

atcoder:abc194_e.title: ABC194 E. Mex Min
levels: The minimum mex over all windows is some value x that is missing from at least one window. When is a value x missing from some window of length M?
x is absent from some length-M window exactly when two consecutive occurrences of x (counting virtual positions −1 and N) leave a gap of at least M cells. The answer is the smallest such x.

1. For every value record its positions; add sentinels −1 and N.
2. x qualifies if some gap next − prev − 1 ≥ M.
3. Print the smallest qualifying x in 0..N. O(N).
(Alternative: slide the window keeping counts and a set of missing values.)

atcoder:abc187_d.title: ABC187 D. Choose Me
levels: Start from the state where you give no speeches. How much does the vote difference change when you speak in one town — and does it depend on the other towns?
A speech in town i changes (Takahashi − Aoki) by 2·A_i + B_i, independently of every other town. So greedily take the towns with the largest 2·A_i + B_i.

1. diff = −ΣA_i.
2. Sort towns by 2·A_i + B_i descending.
3. Add values one by one, counting, until diff > 0 (strictly). Use 64-bit. O(N log N).

atcoder:abc121_d.title: ABC121 D. XOR World
levels: Like range sums, a range XOR can be built from two prefix values. Write out 0 ⊕ 1 ⊕ … ⊕ n for small n — do you see a pattern?
g(n) = 0 ⊕ 1 ⊕ … ⊕ n depends only on n mod 4: it is n, 1, n + 1, 0. Then the answer is g(B) ⊕ g(A − 1).

1. g(n): n%4 == 0 → n, 1 → 1, 2 → n + 1, 3 → 0; define g(−1) = 0.
2. Print g(B) ^ g(A − 1). Watch the A = 0 case. O(1).

atcoder:abc136_e.title: ABC136 E. Max GCD
levels: The operation never changes the total sum S. What does that tell you about any number that divides every element at the end?

Any answer d must divide S, and S has only about a thousand divisors — try them all. For a fixed d, each element is rounded down or up to a multiple of d; the cheapest plan rounds the largest residues up and the smallest down.

1. Enumerate divisors of S in O(√S).
2. For each d: r_i = A_i mod d, sorted ascending; t = Σr_i / d elements must be rounded up (the t largest). Cost = sum of the N − t smallest residues.
3. The largest d with cost ≤ K is the answer. O(√S + D·N log N).

atcoder:abc131_d.title: ABC131 D. Megalomania
levels: If finishing everything is possible, does the order matter? Try swapping two adjacent jobs whose deadlines are out of order.
Earliest-deadline-first is optimal (exchange argument). Sort by deadline and check that every prefix finishes in time.

Sort by B ascending; t = 0; for each job: t += A; if t > B print No. Otherwise print Yes.
Common WA: sorting by A instead of B. O(N log N).

atcoder:dp_f.title: DP F. LCS
levels: Computing the length is the classic part; this task asks you to print an actual string. Which information in the table tells you which move you made?
Standard LCS DP over prefixes, then reconstruct by walking backwards from the bottom-right corner, moving to a neighbour with the same value, or taking the character when you must move diagonally.

1. dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j−1] + 1 if s[i−1] == t[j−1], else max(dp[i−1][j], dp[i][j−1]).
2. From (|s|, |t|): if dp[i][j] == dp[i−1][j] → i−−; else if dp[i][j] == dp[i][j−1] → j−−; else take s[i−1], i−−, j−−.
3. Reverse the collected characters. O(|s|·|t|). Storing strings inside the DP is the usual TLE/MLE.

atcoder:abc128_c.title: ABC128 C. Switches
levels: Look at the constraints first: N ≤ 10. How many on/off combinations of switches exist in total?
Bit brute force: there are only 2^N ≤ 1024 states. For each one, check every bulb's parity condition.

for mask in 0..2^N − 1: for each bulb, count the switches s in its list with bit (s − 1) set; the state is valid if count % 2 == p_i for every bulb → ans++.
Common WA: off-by-one on the 1-indexed switch numbers. O(2^N · N · M).

atcoder:abc146_c.title: ABC146 C. Buy an Integer
levels: If you can afford the integer N, can you also afford every smaller integer? Use that monotonicity.
The price A·N + B·d(N) only increases with N, so binary search the largest affordable N in [0, 10^9].

lo = 0, hi = 10^9 + 1. While hi − lo > 1: mid = (lo + hi) / 2; if A·mid + B·digits(mid) ≤ X then lo = mid else hi = mid. Print lo.
The shop sells nothing above 10^9 — exceeding that cap is the usual WA. Use 64-bit. O(log 10^9).

atcoder:arc096_a.title: ABC095 C. Half and Half
levels: Two AB-pizzas can replace one A-pizza and one B-pizza. How many AB-pizzas could it ever make sense to buy?
Try every even number 2k of AB-pizzas for k = 0 .. max(X, Y) and buy the rest individually. Buying more AB-pizzas than you strictly need can be optimal when C is cheap.
ans = min over k in [0, max(X, Y)] of 2k·C + max(0, X − k)·A + max(0, Y − k)·B. O(max(X, Y)).

atcoder:abc085_d.title: ABC085 D. Katana Thrower
levels: You only ever need to wield one katana — which one? And when is a single throw better than wielding?
Let amax = max a_i. Throw every katana with b_i > amax, largest first, until the monster dies; then wield the best katana for the remaining damage.

1. amax = max a.
2. Sort b descending; for each b > amax: H −= b, cnt++; if H ≤ 0 print cnt.
3. Otherwise print cnt + ceil(H / amax). O(N log N).

codeforces:1934A.title: 1934A · Too Min Too Max
levels: The four chosen indices form a cycle of absolute differences. Which elements of the array can possibly matter for the maximum?
Sort the array. The best cycle alternates small and large values: smallest, largest, second smallest, second largest.
Sort a; print 2·(a[n−1] + a[n−2] − a[0] − a[1]). O(n log n) per test.

codeforces:1985D.title: 1985D · Manhattan Circle
levels: A Manhattan circle on a grid is a diamond. Where is a diamond widest, and how does that relate to its centre?
The centre row is halfway between the topmost and bottommost rows containing '#'; in that row, the centre column is halfway along the '#' segment.

1. top, bottom = first and last rows containing '#'; r = (top + bottom) / 2.
2. In row r, left and right = first and last '#'; c = (left + right) / 2.
3. Print r c (1-indexed). O(nm).

codeforces:1955C.title: 1955C · Inhabitant of the Deep Sea
levels: k can be 10^15, so you cannot simulate attack by attack. How many attacks hit the front in total, and how many hit the back?

The front receives ⌈k/2⌉ attacks and the back ⌊k/2⌋, independently of order. The front sinks the longest prefix with sum ≤ ⌈k/2⌉; the back sinks the longest suffix with sum ≤ ⌊k/2⌋. If k ≥ Σa every ship sinks.

1. If k ≥ Σa print n.
2. front = (k + 1) / 2, back = k / 2.
3. Count prefix ships while the running sum ≤ front; count suffix ships while the running sum ≤ back; print the total. O(n).

codeforces:1923C.title: 1923C · Find B
levels: Every element must change but stay positive. Elements equal to 1 can only go up — where does the extra amount come from?
Each 1 needs at least +1; every element x > 1 can drop to 1 and free x − 1. A subarray is good iff its length is > 1 and Σ(c_i − 1) ≥ the number of ones.
Precompute prefix sums of c and of the count of ones. For a query: len = r − l + 1, s = sum, ones = count. Print YES iff len > 1 and s − len ≥ ones. O(n + q).

codeforces:1991C.title: 1991C · Absolute Zero
levels: Think about parity: what does one operation do to the parities of the elements relative to each other?

If both parities appear, it is impossible — the operation keeps all elements' parities equal to each other or not. Otherwise always pick x = (max + min) / 2: the new maximum is at most half the old range, so about 30 steps suffice.

1. If parities are mixed print −1.
2. Repeat up to 40 times: if all are zero stop; x = (max + min) / 2; record x; a_i = |a_i − x|.
3. Print the recorded operations. O(40·n).

codeforces:1637C.title: 1637C · Andrew and Stones
levels: Every useful operation removes two stones from the middle piles. How many operations does a middle pile of size a need if nothing is wasted?
The answer is Σ⌈a_i/2⌉ over the middle piles, as long as some pile can supply a stone to fix the odd ones. It is impossible if every middle pile is 1, or n = 3 and a_2 is odd.

1. If n == 3 and a_2 is odd → −1.
2. If all of a_2..a_{n−1} are 1 → −1.
3. Otherwise print Σ ⌈a_i/2⌉ for i = 2..n−1 (64-bit). O(n).

codeforces:1760C.title: 1760C · Advantage
levels: For every participant you need the maximum of everyone else. Do you really have to recompute it n times?
Only the maximum and the second maximum matter: everyone compares against the maximum, except the holder of the maximum, who compares against the second maximum.
Find the top two values m1 ≥ m2 (duplicates count separately). For each i print s_i − (s_i == m1 ? m2 : m1). If the maximum appears twice, m2 == m1 and that answer is 0. O(n).

codeforces:2061A.title: 2061A · Kevin and Arithmetic
levels: After Kevin earns a point, s is divided until it becomes odd. Track only parity: which numbers can turn an odd s into an even one?
Put one even number first: s becomes even and scores. From then on s is odd, so every odd number scores and even numbers never do. With no even number at all, the first odd number cannot score.
c1 = number of odd elements. If there is at least one even element print c1 + 1, otherwise print c1 − 1. O(n).

atcoder:abc336_e.title: ADT_ALL_20260728_1 H. Digit Sum Divisible
levels: The digit sum of any n ≤ 10^14 is at most 9·14 = 126. What if you fixed the digit sum before counting?

For each target sum s = 1..126, run a digit DP over the digits of N that tracks (digit sum so far, value mod s, tight). Count numbers whose final digit sum is exactly s and whose remainder is 0. Classic WA: accepting sum ≤ s instead of sum == s, or counting n = 0.

1. For s in 1..126: dp[sum][rem] over positions, with a separate 'still equal to N's prefix' path.
2. Transition with digit d (0..9, capped by N's digit on the tight path): sum += d (skip if > s), rem = (rem·10 + d) mod s.
3. Add dp[s][0] at the end (tight path included).
4. Sum the counts over all s. About 126 × 15 × 126 × 126 × 10 cheap steps — fine with flat arrays.

atcoder:arc086_b.title: ABC081 D. Non-decreasing
levels: If every element is ≥ 0 (or every element is ≤ 0), making the sequence non-decreasing is easy. Can you first make all elements share a sign?

Take the element with the largest absolute value and add it to every element (N operations): now everything has its sign. Then, if all ≥ 0, add a_i to a_{i+1} from left to right; if all ≤ 0, add a_{i+1} to a_i from right to left. Classic WA: choosing the maximum instead of the maximum |a_i|.

1. m = index of max |a_i|.
2. For every y: output (m, y) — all elements now have the sign of a_m.
3. If a_m ≥ 0: for i = 1..N−1 output (i, i+1) (prefix sums grow).
4. Else: for i = N..2 output (i, i−1).
5. That is at most 2N − 1 operations.

atcoder:abc361_f.title: ADT_HARD_20241107_3 I. x = a^b
levels: Perfect squares are easy to count with an exact integer square root. What remains are powers with exponent b ≥ 3 — how large can the base be then?

For b ≥ 3 and N ≤ 10^18 the base is at most 10^6. Enumerate every a^b ≤ N with a ≥ 2, b ≥ 3, drop the ones that are perfect squares (already counted), dedupe with a set, then add isqrt(N). Classic WA: floating-point sqrt near 10^18 — correct it with an integer adjustment loop.

1. ans = isqrt(N) (exact: adjust r while r·r > N or (r+1)² ≤ N).
2. For a = 2..10^6: x = a³; while x ≤ N: if x is not a perfect square, insert x into a set; x *= a (guard overflow with x > N / a).
3. ans += size of the set.

atcoder:arc061_b.title: ABC045 D. Snuke's Coloring
levels: There are about 10^18 3×3 squares, but each black cell lies in at most 9 of them. Count only the squares that contain something.

For every black cell, increment a hash-map counter for each of the ≤ 9 top-left corners (inside [1, H−2] × [1, W−2]) whose square contains it. A square's counter equals its number of black cells. Squares that never appear have 0: (H−2)(W−2) minus the map size. Classic WA: 32-bit overflow in (H−2)(W−2).

1. For each black (a, b): for top-left (x, y) with x in [a−2, a], y in [b−2, b], 1 ≤ x ≤ H−2, 1 ≤ y ≤ W−2: cnt[(x, y)]++.
2. ans[j] = number of keys with cnt = j for j = 1..9.
3. ans[0] = (H−2)(W−2) − (number of keys), in 64-bit.

atcoder:abc328_d.title: ADT_ALL_20260918_2 G. Take ABC
levels: Removing an "ABC" can create a new "ABC" across the gap. Re-scanning from the start each time is O(N²).

Push characters onto a stack; whenever the top three are A, B, C (in that order), pop them. Each character is pushed and popped at most once, and the stack is the final string. Classic TLE: string replace in a loop.

1. st = empty string.
2. For each c in S: st.push(c); if st ends with "ABC", pop 3.
3. Print st.

atcoder:arc081_a.title: ABC071 C. Make a Rectangle
levels: Each side of the rectangle needs two sticks of the same length. Which lengths can be used, and how many times?

Count each length: 2–3 sticks give one pair, 4+ give two pairs (a square is allowed). Take the two largest pairs; the answer is their product, or 0 if there are fewer than two pairs. Classic WA: forgetting the square case, and 32-bit overflow of the area.

1. Count lengths in a map.
2. Build a list of pairs: push the length once if count ≥ 2, twice if count ≥ 4.
3. Sort descending; answer = p[0] · p[1] in 64-bit, or 0.

atcoder:abc112_d.title: ABC112 D. Partition
levels: If the gcd is d, every number is a multiple of d — so their sum M is too, and every number is at least d.
The answer is the largest divisor d of M with d · N ≤ M (use N−1 copies of d and one copy of M − (N−1)d). Enumerate divisors up to √M. Classic TLE: trying every d from M downwards.

1. For i = 1..√M: if M % i == 0, check d = i and d = M / i.
2. Keep the largest d with d · N ≤ M.
3. Print it.

atcoder:arc084_a.title: ABC077 C. Snuke Festival
levels: Fix the middle part. What do you need to know about the upper and lower parts?
Sort A and C. For each B_j, multiply (number of A_i < B_j) by (number of C_k > B_j), both by binary search. Classic WA: using ≤ instead of strict <, and 32-bit overflow (the answer can reach 10^15).

1. Sort A and C.
2. For each b in B: x = lower_bound(A, b) (count < b); y = N − upper_bound(C, b) (count > b).
3. ans += x · y in 64-bit.

atcoder:arc064_a.title: ABC048 C. Boxes and Candies
levels: Process the boxes from left to right. When a_i + a_{i+1} exceeds x, which of the two boxes is it better to eat from?

Greedy: first cap a_1 at x. Then for each i, eat the excess a_i + a_{i+1} − x from the right box a_{i+1} — it also helps the next pair, and the left box is already fixed. Classic WA: forgetting that a_1 alone can exceed x, and 32-bit overflow of the total.

1. If a_1 > x: ans += a_1 − x; a_1 = x.
2. For i = 1..N−1: e = a_i + a_{i+1} − x; if e > 0: ans += e; a_{i+1} −= e.
3. Print ans (64-bit).

atcoder:arc070_b.title: ABC056 D. No Need
levels: If a card is unnecessary, every smaller card is unnecessary too. That monotonicity suggests sorting and a binary search.

Card i is necessary iff the other cards have a subset whose sum lies in [K − a_i, K − 1]. Check it with a subset-sum DP (bitset) over sums < K that skips card i. Sort, then binary search the boundary: O(N·K·log N). Classic WA: cards with a_i ≥ K are always necessary.

1. Sort a ascending.
2. necessary(i): if a_i ≥ K return true; dp = subset sums < K of all cards except i; return any dp[s] for s in [K − a_i, K − 1].
3. Binary search the smallest necessary index t.
4. Answer = t (cards before it are unnecessary).

atcoder:arc060_b.title: ABC044 D. Digit Sum
levels: For small bases, just try them. For a base larger than √n, how many digits does n have in that base?

Brute force b = 2..√n. For b > √n, n has two digits p, q: p + q = s and p(b − 1) = n − s. Try p from √n down to 1 (larger p ⇒ smaller b): b = (n − s)/p + 1 when divisible, then check 0 ≤ q = s − p < b and 1 ≤ p < b. Special cases: s = n ⇒ b = n + 1; s > n ⇒ −1.

1. If s == n: print n + 1. If s > n: print −1.
2. For b = 2..√n: if digit sum of n in base b == s, print b.
3. For p = √n..1: if (n − s) % p == 0: b = (n − s)/p + 1; q = s − p; if b ≥ 2, p < b, 0 ≤ q < b: print b.
4. Otherwise print −1.

atcoder:agc002_b.title: AGC002 B. Box and Ball
levels: Track two things for every box: how many balls it holds, and whether the red ball could be in it.

On a move x → y: if x may hold red, y now may too. Decrement cnt[x] and increment cnt[y]; if cnt[x] becomes 0, x can no longer hold red. The answer counts boxes still marked. Classic WA: clearing x's mark while it still has balls.

1. cnt[i] = 1 for all; red[1] = true.
2. For each (x, y): if red[x]: red[y] = true. cnt[x]−−, cnt[y]++. If cnt[x] == 0: red[x] = false.
3. Print the number of boxes with red[i] = true.

atcoder:abc218_c.title: ADT_ALL_20260727_1 F. Shapes
levels: There are only four rotations. Translation can be handled by aligning both shapes on a reference cell.

Rotate S by 90° up to four times. For each rotation, compare the sets of # cells after shifting both shapes so that their first # in row-major order sits at the origin. The counts of # must also match. Classic WA: comparing raw grids without normalising the translation.

1. If the numbers of # differ: No.
2. norm(G) = list of (r − r0, c − c0) for # cells, where (r0, c0) is the first # in row-major order.
3. For k = 0..3: if norm(S) == norm(T): Yes. Rotate S by 90°.
4. Otherwise No.

atcoder:abc021_c.title: ABC021 C. 正直者の高橋くん
levels: All roads have length 1, so BFS gives the distances. How many shortest paths reach each town?

BFS from a with ways[a] = 1. When looking at an edge u → v with dist[v] == dist[u] + 1, add ways[u] to ways[v] (mod 10^9+7). Classic WA: also adding when v was reached earlier at a smaller distance, or treating the roads as one-way.

1. BFS from a, recording dist.
2. Process vertices in BFS order: for each neighbour v with dist[v] == dist[u] + 1: ways[v] = (ways[v] + ways[u]) mod 1e9+7.
3. Print ways[b].

atcoder:abc015_4.title: ABC015 D. 高橋くんの苦悩
levels: This is a knapsack with an extra limit on how many items you may take.

dp[k][w] = best total importance using k screenshots of total width w. Process items one by one and loop k and w downwards (0/1 knapsack). The answer is the maximum dp[k][w] with k ≤ K and w ≤ W. Classic WA: looping upwards and reusing the same screenshot.

1. dp = −∞ except dp[0][0] = 0.
2. For each (A_i, B_i): for k = K−1..0, for w = W−A_i..0: dp[k+1][w+A_i] = max(dp[k+1][w+A_i], dp[k][w] + B_i).
3. Print the maximum over all dp[k][w].

atcoder:arc035_c.title: ARC035 C. アットコーダー王国の交通事情
levels: Floyd–Warshall once is fine. After adding one road, do you really need to rerun it from scratch?

After adding road (x, y, z), any improved path uses it once: d[i][j] = min(d[i][j], d[i][x] + z + d[y][j], d[i][y] + z + d[x][j]). That is O(N²) per query instead of O(N³). Then sum d[i][j] over i < j. Classic TLE: rerunning Floyd for every query.

1. Floyd–Warshall on the initial graph.
2. For each new road (x, y, z): update every pair with the formula above.
3. Print the sum over i < j (64-bit).

codeforces:1491C.title: 1491C · Pekora and Trampoline
levels: Starting from the first trampoline with strength > 1 is always optimal, and each pass lowers it by 1. Instead of simulating passes, count how many times each trampoline is landed on by earlier passes.

Keep cnt[i] = landings on i coming from earlier starts. Trampoline i needs max(0, S_i − 1 − cnt[i]) new passes. One pass at strength t lands on i + t, so its passes land once on each of i+2..i+S_i — add them with a difference array. Surplus landings cnt[i] − (S_i − 1) carry over to i + 1. Classic TLE: simulating every pass in O(N).

1. ans = 0; diff = zeros.
2. For i = 1..N: cnt[i] += running sum of diff.
3. ans += max(0, S_i − 1 − cnt[i]).
4. Mark landings on [i+2, min(N, i+S_i)] with +1 (difference array).
5. If cnt[i] > S_i − 1: carry cnt[i] − (S_i − 1) to cnt[i+1].
6. Print ans (64-bit).

codeforces:1401F.title: 1401F · Reverse and Swap
levels: Both operations only permute positions inside a segment tree over 2^n leaves. Can each one be described as a change to how indices are read?

Reverse(k) flips bits 0..k−1 of every index; Swap(k) flips bit k. Keep a global xor mask: reverse(k) → mask ^= 2^k − 1, swap(k) → mask ^= 2^k. Point updates go to position x ^ mask. For sums, descend the tree and swap the two children at level j when bit j of the mask is set. Classic WA: applying the mask to point updates but not to the range descent.

1. Build a sum segment tree on the original array (0-indexed, 2^n leaves).
2. Replace(x, v): update leaf (x − 1) ^ mask.
3. Reverse(k): mask ^= (1 << k) − 1. Swap(k): mask ^= 1 << k.
4. Sum(l, r): recurse from the root; a node whose children differ in index bit j visits them in swapped order when bit j of mask is set (map the query range through the same swaps).

codeforces:445E.title: 445E · DZY Loves Colors
levels: Painting turns a whole range into a single colour. How many single-colour segments can paint operations destroy in total?

Segment tree storing the sum of colourfulness (with a lazy add) and the node's colour if it is uniform (else −1). A paint recurses only until it reaches uniform nodes fully inside [l, r]: add |x − c| · len there via the lazy tag, then set the colour to x. The number of visited nodes is amortised O((n + m) log n). Classic WA: 32-bit sums.

1. Node: sum, addLazy (per unit), color (−1 if mixed).
2. paint(node, l, r, x): if node is inside [l, r] and color != −1: addLazy += |x − color|, sum += |x − color| · len, color = x; return. Otherwise push down, recurse, pull up (color = children's colour if equal, else −1).
3. query(l, r): standard range sum with lazy push.

codeforces:1093E.title: 1093E · Intersection of Permutations
levels: Map each value v to the point (position of v in a, position of v in b). What does a query look like in that picture?

A query counts points in the rectangle [la, ra] × [lb, rb]; swapping b_x and b_y moves two points. You need dynamic 2D rectangle counting: a BIT over x whose nodes hold order-statistic sets of y, offline CDQ divide and conquer, or sqrt decomposition. Classic TLE: intersecting sets per query.

1. posA[v] = index of v in a; point for v is (posA[v], posB[v]).
2. Query(la, ra, lb, rb) = count(ra, lb..rb) − count(la − 1, lb..rb) with a BIT of sorted structures (or process all events offline with CDQ).
3. Swap(x, y): remove the points of values b_x and b_y, swap them, insert them back.
4. Each operation is O(log² n).
